catalogue_metadata.scope_notes: Extraction based on the provided manifest, directory tree, and key symbols. Full source content was not available for deep static analysis.
analysis_limits: No full source code traversal was possible; evidence is limited to file paths, symbols, and manifest metadata.
Agentic AI orchestration patterns were intentionally excluded from this catalogue.
Some patterns are inferred from class names, module layout, and CLI/runner structure rather than verified inline implementations.

system_map.overview: CAS Runner is a Python CLI that bootstraps a governance-aware workspace, executes a flow through pluggable services, and produces knowledge artifacts. The structural architecture separates the CLI/application layer from governance domain models and infrastructure clients via service classes and typed Pydantic models.

layers.name: Presentation
layers.purpose: Command-line entrypoint and user-facing dashboard health reporting.

layers.name: Application
layers.purpose: Orchestrate flows, state transitions, compliance checks, and workspace setup.

layers.name: Domain
layers.purpose: Typed domain models for governance records, compliance findings, skill evaluations, and health metrics.

layers.name: Infrastructure
layers.purpose: External adapters, file system bootstrap operations, and generic LLM client abstractions.

containers.name: CLI
containers.purpose: Parse commands and delegate to runner or bootstrap routines.

containers.name: FlowRunner
containers.purpose: Executes the main flow, coordinating services and clients.

containers.name: GovernanceActionService
containers.purpose: Provides a service facade for governance actions.

containers.name: GovernanceActionEngine
containers.purpose: Evaluates and executes governance state transitions using a transition registry.

containers.name: ComplianceEngine
containers.purpose: Evaluates repository or workspace compliance and produces findings.

containers.name: LiteLLMClient
containers.purpose: Production adapter for LLM access via LiteLLM.

containers.name: MockLLMClient
containers.purpose: Deterministic test/dry-run adapter for LLM access.

containers.name: Bootstrap
containers.purpose: Initializes workspaces, merges governance blocks, and installs skills/config files.

key_components: Pydantic domain models in governance/models.py and skills/models.py
dependencies: cli.py depends on FlowRunner and bootstrap routines
FlowRunner depends on governance services and LLM client abstractions
GovernanceActionService depends on GovernanceActionEngine and TransitionRegistry
ComplianceEngine depends on domain models for compliance findings
Domain models are framework-free Pydantic schemas used across service boundaries
Bootstrap depends on file system operations and YAML/JSON merging

patterns.name: Pydantic Domain Entity Modeling
patterns.summary: Domain concepts are represented as Pydantic models with explicit fields, enums, and nested structures, enabling validation and serialization across service boundaries.
patterns.intent: Establish a strongly typed domain model for governance records, compliance findings, skill evaluations, and health metrics.
patterns.context: CAS needs to persist and exchange multiple kinds of structured knowledge artifacts while keeping a shared domain vocabulary across the CLI, runner, and services.
forces: Multiple domain object kinds require consistent validation.
Data moves between files, services, and possibly external processes.
Ad hoc dictionaries become unmaintainable as schemas evolve.
patterns.solution: Define dedicated Pydantic models for each domain aggregate and value object, using enums for statuses and nested models for metrics and results.
implementation_signals: models.py files contain multiple Pydantic BaseModel subclasses.
Status and result types are modeled as enums or typed literals.
Service methods accept and return model instances rather than raw dicts.

evidence.note: Governance domain is modeled as a set of typed Pydantic records.
Skill evaluation domain uses structured models for suites and reports.
Health status is represented as a typed domain model with pure calculation functions.

benefits: Consistent validation and serialization across components.
Explicit contracts for service boundaries.
Easier testing and maintenance of domain logic.
costs: Boilerplate when adding new models or fields.
Schema changes can ripple through services and persisted artifacts.
failure_modes: Over-coupling to schema details if models are used as universal DTOs.
Large model files can become hard to navigate.

patterns.name: LLM Client Adapter Strategy
patterns.summary: The FlowRunner depends on an LLM client abstraction with interchangeable production and mock implementations.
patterns.intent: Decouple orchestration from concrete LLM vendors and support deterministic testing and offline execution.
patterns.context: Commands need model access but should not hardcode a vendor-specific client, enabling both live and mock execution.
forces: LLM providers can change or require different configuration.
Automated tests need deterministic outputs.
Users may run in environments without network access.
patterns.solution: Define a common client interface or protocol, implement LiteLLMClient for production, and MockLLMClient for deterministic scenarios.
implementation_signals: Multiple client classes in an llm/ package with similar method shapes.
Runner or services accept the client as a dependency rather than instantiating a vendor-specific class directly.
A mock client is used for dry-run or test paths.

evidence.note: Production adapter wraps the LiteLLM package.
Mock adapter supports deterministic behavior without an external service.
FlowRunner consumes the client abstraction during flow execution.

benefits: Vendor logic is isolated from application flow.
Tests can run without external LLM APIs.
New providers can be added by implementing the same interface.
costs: Vendor-specific features may be underrepresented in the shared interface.
failure_modes: Interface becomes a leaky abstraction if vendor-specific options are threaded through.
Mismatches between mock and real behavior can hide issues.

patterns.name: Transition Registry State Machine
patterns.summary: Governance actions are modeled as state transitions registered in a dedicated registry, and executed by a central engine.
patterns.intent: Centralize and enforce allowed state changes instead of scattering transition logic across services.
patterns.context: Governance records can move through lifecycle states, and the validity of an action depends on the current state.
forces: State logic can become complex and hard to audit.
New transitions should be added without modifying core action logic.
Invalid transitions must be rejected consistently.
patterns.solution: Use a TransitionRegistry to map allowed source states and actions, and delegate execution to a GovernanceActionEngine.
implementation_signals: A class named TransitionRegistry exists alongside the engine.
GovernanceActionService delegates to the engine rather than implementing state checks inline.
The engine is used by services as the single entrypoint for actions.

evidence.note: State transitions and engine execution are explicitly modeled.
Service layer uses the engine, keeping transition logic in the engine/registry.

benefits: Transition rules are explicit and auditable.
Adding new state transitions is localized.
Invalid transitions can be reported consistently.
costs: Requires a mental model of the registry/engine indirection.
May be overkill for very simple state logic.
failure_modes: Missing registry entries can cause runtime errors for valid-looking actions.
Registry can become large and need periodic maintenance.

patterns.name: Compliance Engine Rule Evaluation
patterns.summary: A dedicated compliance engine evaluates governance rules and produces typed findings and metrics.
patterns.intent: Separate compliance checking from domain operations and standardize the output of compliance assessments.
patterns.context: The system needs to assess workspaces or repositories against governance rules and report violations in a consistent format.
forces: Rule checks can grow independently from core flow logic.
Findings must be comparable across different governance dimensions.
The engine needs to be testable without running the whole CLI.
patterns.solution: Encapsulate rule evaluation in a ComplianceEngine that returns ComplianceFinding and ComplianceMetrics models.
implementation_signals: A class named ComplianceEngine exists in the governance package.
Compliance findings and metrics are typed models.
The engine is referenced as a discrete component in the service layer.

evidence.note: Engine encapsulates rule evaluation and finding generation.
Typed models represent the output of compliance checks.

benefits: Consistent reporting of violations.
Rule logic is isolated and easier to test.
Metrics can be aggregated from typed results.
costs: The engine may become large as rule complexity grows.
Requires careful modeling to handle all finding types.
failure_modes: Engine can become a god-class if rules are not further modularized.
Findings can become over-structured for simple rule checks.

patterns.name: Pure Function Health Metric
patterns.summary: Dashboard health is computed by pure functions that map observations to a HealthStatus with explanatory reasons.
patterns.intent: Keep health logic deterministic, side-effect free, and easy to unit test.
patterns.context: The dashboard needs to display an aggregate health state for governance or skill areas without coupling to rendering or IO.
forces: Health calculations should be reproducible and explainable.
Rendering should not be blocked by complex domain logic.
Reasons for a health status are needed for user trust and debugging.
patterns.solution: Implement calculate_health and get_health_reasons as pure functions over typed inputs, returning a HealthStatus value.
implementation_signals: A health_model.py module contains only domain functions and types.
Health status is an enum or typed value.
The dashboard imports these functions rather than embedding logic in UI code.

evidence.note: Health computation is separated from dashboard rendering and IO.

benefits: Deterministic and testable health logic.
Clear separation between domain calculation and presentation.
Reasons can be shown directly to users.
costs: Health logic may need additional context as the dashboard evolves.
Pure functions can oversimplify complex health signals.
failure_modes: Missing context can lead to misleading health statuses.
Health reason generation may duplicate logic if not maintained centrally.

patterns.name: Workspace Bootstrap Merge or Copy
patterns.summary: Workspace initialization merges governance blocks into configuration files and copies or symlinks skill assets without destructive overwrites.
patterns.intent: Create a reproducible, versionable workspace setup while preserving user customizations.
patterns.context: A new or existing project needs CAS governance files, Claude settings, and skill assets installed without clobbering local configuration.
forces: Users may have existing configuration that should not be overwritten.
Skill files need to be linked or copied for discoverability.
Setup should be repeatable across machines and CI environments.
patterns.solution: Use merge_cas_governance_block and merge_claude_settings for configuration merging, and _create_symlink_or_copy for skill installation.
implementation_signals: Bootstrap module contains functions named with merge or link semantics.
An init_workspace or bootstrap entrypoint coordinates the setup steps.
File system operations are explicit and handle both copy and symlink modes.

evidence.note: Workspace setup is decomposed into merge/copy steps and a top-level initializer.

benefits: Preserves existing user configurations.
Setup is idempotent and safer to run repeatedly.
Symlinks keep skill sources centralized while exposing them in workspaces.
costs: Symlink behavior can differ across platforms and file systems.
failure_modes: Partial merges can lead to malformed config files if not transactional.
Symlink creation may require permissions or fail on Windows without developer mode.

patterns.name: Workflow Validation Gate
patterns.summary: A standalone validation script enforces CI/CD workflow hygiene through named check functions before changes are accepted.
patterns.intent: Keep GitHub Actions workflow definitions consistent, reproducible, and free of known configuration anti-patterns.
patterns.context: The repository contains multiple workflow files, and maintainers need automated guardrails to prevent drift.
forces: Several workflows can evolve independently.
Common mistakes like hardcoding or unpinned installers are easy to introduce.
Reviewers need clear, automated signals rather than manual workflow inspection.
patterns.solution: Create a validate_workflows.py script with discrete check_* functions for YAML syntax, pinned installers, hardcoding, unreachable dry runs, and retired workflow cleanup.
implementation_signals: A validation script lives under specs/ or similar spec directory.
Checks are named with a check_ prefix and each addresses one concern.
A main() function aggregates and runs all checks.

evidence.note: Validation is decomposed into a main gate with named check functions for each workflow concern.

benefits: Early detection of workflow anti-patterns.
Policy is encoded in reusable, testable functions.
Reviewers can focus on substantive changes rather than all workflow details.
costs: Additional script must be maintained as workflow expectations change.
Checks may become too strict or stale if not updated with workflow style evolution.
failure_modes: False positives can block unrelated changes.
If new workflow anti-patterns appear, the gate must be extended.

anti_patterns.name: Hardcoded CI/CD Configuration Values
symptoms: Workflow files contain literal environment names, artifact paths, or step identifiers that should be parameters.
A validation check named check_zero_hardcoding exists in the repository's workflow validation script.
impact: Reduces portability across branches, environments, and forks.
Makes workflow maintenance error-prone when copying steps between jobs.
suggested_remediation: Extract hardcoded values into repository variables, environment variables, or typed workflow inputs.

anti_patterns.name: Unpinned Installer Versions
symptoms: Installer actions or setup scripts do not specify exact versions, allowing floating updates.
A validation check named check_no_unpinned_installers exists in the workflow validation script.
impact: Builds can become non-reproducible when a new installer version changes behavior.
Intermittent CI failures may be difficult to trace to an unpinned dependency.
suggested_remediation: Pin installer and action versions to a specific commit/tag or use a lockfile mechanism.

anti_patterns.name: Unreachable Dry Run Branch
symptoms: Dry-run logic exists behind conditions that are never true in the workflow.
A validation check named check_no_unreachable_dry_run exists in the workflow validation script.
impact: Dead code paths mislead operators into thinking dry-run mode is available when it is not.
Maintainers may waste time debugging an impossible branch.
suggested_remediation: Remove unreachable branches or update the conditions so the dry-run path is achievable and tested.

anti_patterns.name: Retired Workflow Left in Place
symptoms: Workflow files remain in the repository after they have been replaced or decommissioned.
A validation check named check_retired_workflow exists in the workflow validation script.
impact: Creates confusion about which workflows are active.
Can result in wasted CI runs or accidental re-enablement.
suggested_remediation: Delete retired workflows and update references to the replacement workflow.

cross_cutting_concerns.description: Pydantic models are used consistently in governance, skills, and health domains to validate data at service boundaries.
MockLLMClient and pure health functions support deterministic verification of flows that otherwise depend on external LLM APIs.
Bootstrap operations merge configuration and use copy-vs-symlink strategies to avoid destructive overwrites during workspace initialization.
A dedicated validation script enforces workflow-level constraints such as no hardcoded values, pinned installers, and no retired workflow files.
OpenTelemetry dependencies are declared in the project manifest, indicating a cross-cutting concern for tracing and metrics in executed flows.
